title: Human Expert Evaluation of Agentic AI for EO, form F10
description:
Thank you for helping us evaluate the performance of different LLMs in Agentic AI frameworks for EO!

WHAT THIS IS
We built a benchmark to test the performance of different LLMs in agentic settings. This evaluation form is to compare the answers given by these LLMs when answering a question using different tools related to the agentic framework that we built - including different EO endpoints (Copernicus/Sentinel, Landsat), ERA5 climate data, EO Dashboard narratives, ESA science strategy documents, GIS analysis and scientific literature search.

You will be given 10 questions, and for each question you see every anonymous answer that assistant actually produced for it -- usually several, occasionally just one if only one assistant answered that particular question.

WHAT YOU DO
(About 59 minutes for this form -- your progress is saved in this browser, so it's fine to do this over more than one sitting.) The form will guide you through it, but for every question you will
1. Rate how relevant and realistic the question is for EO users.
2. Score the accuracy of each answer shown.
3. If there's more than one answer, rank them all from best to worst (skip this step when only one answer is shown -- there's nothing to compare it to).

HOW TO JUDGE ACCURACY
Judge scientific and domain correctness, and whether the answer addresses every part of the question. A minority of answers (marked "▣ image" next to the answer letter) include the actual image the assistant looked at -- check the description against it directly. For every other answer you cannot open the files or images it says it produced: treat claims that you find implausible or unsupported as errors. Do not reward length or formatting. If you cannot judge a question, say so in the comment field and give your best estimate.

Answers were produced automatically and may contain errors. Local file paths were removed from the answers. Long answers are collapsed by default — click an answer to expand it.

PRIVACY
Your name is recorded so we can follow up if needed, and is not shown to other experts. Responses are used only for the research evaluation of this benchmark and are reported in aggregate. Participation is voluntary; you can stop at any time by closing the page.

profile_fields.title: Name
profile_fields.help: So we know who a response came from. Not shown to other experts.

profile_fields.title: How would you rate your Earth Observation expertise?
Which areas are you experienced in?
choices: Climate and atmospheric data (ERA5, trace gases)

profile_fields.title: Consent
choices: I agree that my responses are used for the research evaluation of this benchmark.

relevance.title: How relevant and realistic is this question for EO users (researchers, analysts, practitioners)?
relevance.help: 1 = not relevant or unrealistic; 3 = plausible but marginal or somewhat artificial; 5 = highly relevant and realistic.

accuracy.title: Accuracy: how correct and complete is each answer?
accuracy.help: 1 = incorrect or unusable; 2 = mostly incorrect or major omissions; 3 = partially correct or incomplete; 4 = mostly correct, minor issues; 5 = correct and complete. Equal scores are allowed.

ranking.title: Ranking: order all answers from best to worst.
ranking.help: Drag, or use the arrows, to put the best answer at the top and the worst at the bottom. Ties are not allowed.

familiarity.title: How familiar are you with the topic of this question?

comment.title: Comment (optional)
comment.help: For example: an error you spotted, why a question is not relevant, or that you could not judge it.

Identify a representative coastal location discussed in a narrative, retrieve ERA5 monthly mean sea surface temperature within a 2° × 2° region around that location for three representative years from different decades, and compute the multi-year mean SST field to characterize typical ocean temperature conditions.

answers.text:
The multi-year mean sea surface temperature (SST) field for the 2° × 2° region around 8°S, 80°W (near the coast of Peru) has been successfully computed. Here is the final output:

Output File
• File Path: mean_sst_1990_2000_2010_peru_coast.nc

Steps to Generate the File (Recap)
1. Convert SST from Kelvin to Celsius for all three years (1990, 2000, 2010).
2. Clip the data to the bounding box:
   • North: -6.0°
   • South: -10.0°
   • East: -79.0°
   • West: -81.0°
3. Compute the multi-year mean SST for the three years combined.
4. Save the result as a NetCDF file.

• Python (xarray, matplotlib, cartopy)
• QGIS (for spatial analysis)

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Load the file

Plot the mean SST

plt.title("Multi-Year Mean SST (1990, 2000, 2010) - Coastal Peru")

items.label: Cross-agent Synthesis
items.question: Search the EO Dashboard for a narrative about flooding. Identify the affected area it discusses, then download Sentinel-1 SAR images of that area before and after the flood event. Analyse changes in radar backscatter to identify newly inundated areas and describe the spatial extent of flooding.

answers.text:
Methodology for Flood Mapping in the Horn of Africa Using Sentinel-1 GRD Data

Sentinel-1 SAR (Synthetic Aperture Radar) data is highly effective for flood mapping due to its ability to penetrate clouds and operate day and night. Flooded areas appear as low backscatter regions in SAR images because water acts as a specular reflector, reflecting the radar signal away from the sensor. Below is a step-by-step methodology to identify flooding using Sentinel-1 GRD (Ground Range Detected) data in the Horn of Africa.

1. Data Acquisition
Data Source
• Sentinel-1 GRD Data:
  • Product Type: Ground Range Detected (GRD) Level-1.
  • Polarization: VV (Vertical transmit, Vertical receive) or VV+VH (dual-pol) for better discrimination of water and land.
  • Resolution: High-resolution (e.g., 10m) for detailed flood mapping.
  • Swath: Interferometric Wide (IW) mode for most land areas.
  • Temporal Resolution: 6–12 days (depending on orbit).
  • Data Access:
    • Copernicus Open Access Hub (https://scihub.copernicus.eu/ (https://scihub.copernicus.eu/))
    • Google Earth Engine (GEE) (for automated processing)
    • Sentinel Hub (https://www.sentinel-hub.com/ (https://www.sentinel-hub.com/))

Region of Interest (ROI)
• Horn of Africa: Focus on flood-prone regions like:
  • Sudan (White Nile, Blue Nile, and River Nile)
  • South Sudan (Sudd wetlands, Nile River)
  • Ethiopia (Omo River, Baro River)
  • Somalia (Shabelle and Juba Rivers)
  • Kenya (Lake Victoria, Tana River)
  • Eritrea (coastal and riverine areas)

Time Period
• Pre-flood: Select a reference image before the flood event (e.g., 1–2 months prior).
• Post-flood: Select an image during or immediately after the flood event.
• Additional Images: Use multiple pre- and post-flood images to account for seasonal variations.

2. Preprocessing
Step 1: Radiometric Calibration
• Convert DN (Digital Number) to σ⁰ (sigma naught), the radar backscatter coefficient, which represents the actual radar reflectivity.
• Formula:
  \[
  \sigma^0 = 10 \cdot \log_{10}(DN^2) + CF
  \]
  where CF is the calibration factor (provided in the product metadata).

Step 2: Terrain Correction (Geometric Correction)
• Apply Range-Doppler Terrain Correction to correct for:
  • Topographic distortions (layover, foreshortening, shadow).
  • Geometric distortions (Earth’s curvature, sensor angle).
• Use a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) (e.g., SRTM 30m or TanDEM-X) for terrain correction.
• Tools:
  • SNAP (Sentinel Application Platform) (ESA)
  • Google Earth Engine (GEE)

Here is the full text content of an EO Dashboard narrative about aerosols or atmospheric particulate matter, focusing on the Hunga volcano eruption (2022) and its aerosol plumes:

Narrative Title:
Tracking aerosol plumes from Hunga eruption of 2022

Summary:
This narrative examines the aerosol plumes produced by the Hunga volcano eruption in January 2022, which injected unprecedented amounts of water vapor and aerosols into the stratosphere. Key topics include:
• The radiative impact of volcanic aerosols on global climate.
• The unique warming effect of water vapor in the stratosphere, unlike the cooling effects observed in past eruptions (e.g., Pinatubo in 1991).
• The use of satellite data interpolation to track the plume’s dispersion.

The work was developed during the 3rd Earth System Science Challenge (ESA ESRIN Science Hub, 2024) by a team from Sorbonne Université, Académie Spatiale, and IPGP using the DeepESDL platform.

Key Sections:

1. Volcanoes and Climate
• Explores how volcanic eruptions alter global temperatures.
• References the Pinatubo eruption (1991), which caused a 0.6°C global cooling due to sulfate aerosols.

2. The Hunga Eruption (2022)
• Highlights the exceptional water vapor injection into the stratosphere.
• Notes that unlike past eruptions, Hunga’s plume may have caused short-term warming (Sellitto et al., 2022).
• Emphasizes the role of satellite data in tracking aerosol dispersion.

3. Methodology
• Uses temporal interpolation of satellite observations to model plume movement.
• Data and code are openly available via the DeepESDL platform.

4. Visualizations
• Interactive maps of the Hunga volcano and aerosol plume trajectories.
• Logos of contributing institutions (Sorbonne Université, IPGP, Académie Spatiale).

Full Narrative Access:
The complete narrative, including interactive maps and references, is available here:
 Read Full Narrative (https://ESA-eodashboards.github.io/eodashboard-narratives/hunga_tonga_aerosol_plumes.md)

1. N1_SO2: Sulfur dioxide measurements.
2. N1_NO2: Nitrogen dioxide measurements.
3. S5P-L3GRD-AAI-DAY: Absorbing Aerosol Index (AAI) from Sentinel-5P.

Theme: Atmosphere

Full Text Content:
The narrative describes how NASA scientists use the Ozone Monitoring Instrument (OMI) on the Aura satellite to monitor air quality from space. Specifically, it focuses on:

• Nitrogen Dioxide ($\text{NO}_2$): Emitted from burning fossil fuels (cars, trucks, power plants).
• Sulfur Dioxide ($\text{SO}_2$): Produced primarily by burning coal, leading to acid rain and haze.
• Aerosols: The OMI instrument also provides unique insights into aerosols such as smoke, dust, and sulfates.

The story highlights a trilateral collaboration between ESA, NASA, and JAXA to track these pollutants in the northeastern regions of India, China, and the U.S. over the last two decades to understand the impact of human activities versus natural processes on air quality.
